936.t: The list exercise and why not to have a safety net
936.s: He has students list everything they could do in music, the skills each needs and how to practice them; he argues against falling back on teaching.
936.q: A little sharp is better, or it would really be a downer. There’s that, then the other things, I’ll go through a week of what I do. And I’ll say okay, now I want you to write down all the things you could do as a musician. Shows, club dates, weddings, this, that, boom, boom, boom. Make that list.…

217.t: Advice to young musicians: enjoy what you do
217.s: He says to love the work and refuses things he does not want to do.
217.q: No, well the first thing you have to do, you have to enjoy what you do. You have to enjoy what you do and love it. And I think if you enjoy it, that’ll take care of itself, you know what I mean? You’ve got to enjoy it first and have fun with it. Otherwise you’re going through life—

68.t: Best band, and advice to young musicians
68.s: Tate calls Basie the best swinging band and advises young players to practice, listen and stay hungry.
68.q: Swinging. I thought so. I thought it was. Because it could, it could basically sit right here in this room and swing like a dog, and the room didn’t have to be no bigger than this. And he could keep the band down and be swinging like crazy. And I thought he had, I thought he had about the best…

975.t: Advice for a young pianist who wants a music career
975.s: Weber answers Rowe about a high school student: you must love it and give up everything, but you never know who breaks through.
975.q: What’s motivating him to play right now? I mean if someone has, I mean some musicians come from a place where they have stage mothers or fathers who will go on to be the next American Idol. And other kids, they can’t even help it, they just love to play so much that they’re naturally inclined to do…

672.s: She tells young singers to sing anywhere, work small rooms and learn their craft before people.
672.q: Sing anyplace they ask you to sing. Use your voice. Work. Learn your craft. And you can’t learn your craft at home. You need to work those little rooms. You need to put your music in front of people, not in a studio. You need to work. And this is something they’ve gotten away from. And we need…

408.s: Woods advises only those with no choice to pursue jazz, to keep the joy, and to take a year off to travel.
408.q: Advice for young jazzmen. No. I figure that if they’re going to do it, no matter what I say they’re going to do it. It’s for those ones in between, those ones that aren’t really sure, those are the ones I worry about. I mean I think jazz is only for those that have no choice. I think if you’re a…

588.s: She says to see your inherent beauty and that artists are powerful.
588.q: Well, it sounds real simple and I think it really is, but it's not really that simple. Mama taught me this and I wrote this song and I said that she did. Mama told me of a beauty that is made of purest gold, one the weather will not tarnish, one that never will grow old. She said beauty comes from…

223.s: Be honest in the music, aim for organic pieces, and sing yesterday's work before continuing.
223.q: Just keep in mind that your music is an expression of you and try to have the best life you can have and the best intentions, because I think it will come out in your music. Try to get as much variety as you can, as much accomplishment, and to be honest. No technical talk, because I think that‟s…

133.t: Parting shots: advice to students to choose a path and stay on it
133.s: Asked for closing words, Walton tells young musicians to keep striving for excellence and stay on one path, and jokes about playing D.C. versus Beirut.
133.ch: NEA Jazz Master, family and the future
133.q: Yeah. Well uh, if uh you would uh be interested in uh what I would have to say to uh a student of the music now uh, uh because I do get a lot of questions uh, people uh, in uh uh generations that precede me uh, uh: How should I pursue this or that and uh and uh one basic thing that I say is uh,…

101.t: Advice to students: only take out what you put in
101.s: Hard work, the bank-account analogy, and 'the difference between a groove and a grave'.
101.q: I’d like to leave a thought with the students who are getting involved, to impress upon them the fact that you have to really approach what you believe in diligently enough to work hard at it, because nothing comes easy. It like, you only take out what you put in. We always help kids understand…

134.t: Passing on knowledge and not keeping jazz secret
134.s: His present goal is to help young players, he says, and jazz knowledge has been kept secret.
134.q: My current goal is to, whatever little knowledge I got by me being present around young cats, I can help them. That’s my present goal, if I have one.

491.t: Preparing so you are ready when opportunity knocks
491.s: Golson says talent also needs opportunity, so musicians should keep preparing; Brown quotes Jimmy Jam, and Golson speaks of making time your confederate.
491.ch: Advice, education and the evolution of jazz
491.q: without the arrogance – to go ahead. If you’ve got the talent, you can parlay that talent. But it doesn’t happen overnight. The other element in the equation – you could have all the talent in the world – the other element in the equation is opportunity. If you don’t have opportunity, it’s…

371.t: Advice to young musicians and close of the interview
371.s: Master the instrument and theory, avoid drugs, liquor and smoking, and stay healthy.
371.ch: Thad, recent work, outlook and advice
371.q: (Laughs) Well, I guess my comments would mostly be for advice. I would advise,… You see I think the future of our music, jazz, it belongs to the younger people who are entering the field, or who are contemplating entering the field. I would advise them, first of all, to be proficient on their…

704.t: Soul and science, discipline and delayed gratification
704.s: Jones says emotion needs the backing of scientific training, whether for a pianist, surgeon or businessman, and that discipline serves your life: get the pain out of the way first.
704.q: But see, the thing is, it’s mechanics. That’s the soul and the science. Every time there’s some emotion lotion, which guides the science, there’s some brain strain that’s backing up – the emotion’s backed up with the science. That’s whether you’re a piano player or a surgeon – neurosurgeon – or…

555.t: Final advice: stay with the music
555.s: Liston says to study and do it or not, not to get hung up on people before lifelong love, and that she kept to her music.
555.q: Until you know that somebody that’s going to be yours and you’re going to be his, and you’re going to be lifetime or something together.

528.t: Advice to young musicians: get a lawyer
528.s: Brown asks for advice; Tyner says get a lawyer, echoing Louis Armstrong.
528.ch: Steinway, Blue Note, awards and wrap-up
528.q: Because you have to know I mean there is a lot of people that want you to do this, want you to do that record, want you to do this-

92.t: Advice to young musicians: study the heritage
92.s: Collins urges young players to listen to earlier recordings, since what they do extends what was done before.
92.ch: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
92.q: Now, I -- it's just -- one thing I want to say is for the young musician we have some fine young musicians now, on all instruments. That's piano, drums, guitar, trumpet, whatever. But for them I think they should realize that what they are doing now is essentially an extension of what has been done…

388.t: Offer to help young musicians; age 65 with the World's Greatest Jazz Band
388.s: Leeman gives his phone number, says he wants to help anyone interested, and says he still plays strongly for an hour and a half at age 65.
388.q: : And I'm interested -- if I can help anybody in any way, I've got a few tricks and a few things to talk about. Maybe I can help somebody, maybe they would like, out of curiosity, to talk to me. But it'd be nice if they could see me work, still. I'm 65 years old -- I'd like to have them see me…

149.s: Practice, meet good people, and let young players sit in.
149.q: In other words, besides, what you remember I was saying about my practice. That's what I was thinking. Practice. [Laughs] Well, that's one of the big things. Then, get around with, go around and listen and hear and meet the good people in the business that like to talk. I met some nice young…

31.t: Advice to young people: take advantage of opportunities
31.s: Whaley credits his mother for making him study and recalls starving eight months in New York.
31.ch: Working with Duke and final reflections
31.q: Well, see, I had a very good mother, and she kept us in line, she made us study and take advantage of your opportunities. If you don't take advantage of your opportunities, you'll never get nowhere.

413.t: Being a musician as a way of life
413.s: The trumpet, the embouchure and why one becomes a musician.
413.q: When I was young it was like that. Anybody could get a job. Now kids are going to Julliard and God, these kids are coming out of the school playing better than the best in my day, and these kids are not getting anyplace. Being a musician -- you know, as I look back on it, it's a philosophy, a way…

7.s: Thomas urges finding where one's talent lies, citing student Oscar Cohen who went to Joe Glaser's mailroom, and his son the artist.
7.q: To find out what your talent is, what you're best in. It's good that you like it, but if you find out what your talent is, proceed in it.
